changes.after: A program follows instructions. WriteLine shows text on a new line.

before: A program is a sequence of instructions. Code is those instructions written in a language. This first program displays two pieces of text in order.
Text inside double quotes is a string: the quotes mark its boundaries and are not displayed. A statement is one instruction; a semicolon ends each output statement here.

System.Console.WriteLine displays its argument and then starts a new line. The argument is the value between the parentheses. The dots select WriteLine inside Console inside System; keep the capitalization as shown.
These are top-level statements: the C# project supplies the entry-point structure, so you can begin with the output instructions. The second statement runs after the first.

This course uses reading and understanding checks, not an in-browser compiler. The code is a complete optional local example. A compiler translates source code into a form a runtime or computer can execute.

For optional local work, install a supported .NET SDK (the tools for building and running C#), create a console project with dotnet new console -n TinyStudy, and replace its Program.cs with this example. Run dotnet run --project TinyStudy. These are terminal commands, not C# statements. The examples use top-level statements, supported since C# 9. This course does not claim it executed your local project.
after: A program is a set of instructions for a computer to follow. Code is those instructions written in a programming language. Here, that language is C#.
A string is text inside double quotes. The quotes show where the text starts and ends; they are not printed. A statement is an instruction. The semicolon ends each statement in this example.
System.Console.WriteLine shows a value and then starts a new line. The value inside the parentheses is called an argument. Keep the spelling and capital letters as shown.
You can write these instructions directly at the top level of a modern C# console project. The compiler creates the program's starting method for you. The first instruction runs before the second.
A compiler translates code into a form that can run. The .NET runtime runs this compiled C# program. CodeQuest shows the example and an understanding check; it does not run C# in the browser.

For optional local practice, install the .NET 10 SDK: tools for building and running C#. In a terminal, run dotnet new console -n TinyStudy. Replace TinyStudy/Program.cs with the example. Then run dotnet run --project TinyStudy. These commands go in the terminal, not in Program.cs.

before.question: If the two output statements instead contain "Moon" first and "Sun" second, what is displayed?
choices: Moon then Sun, on separate lines.
Sun then Moon, because the last statement runs first.
The quote marks and instruction names, rather than the text.
before.explanation: Output statements run in sequence. Each writes its text then a newline; quote marks are code boundaries, not displayed characters.

after.question: The first WriteLine contains "Moon" and the second contains "Sun". What is shown?
choices: Moon, then Sun, on separate lines.
The quote marks and instruction names.
after.explanation: The statements run in order. Each prints its text and starts a new line.
